name: Teesport
title: Teesport UTM: Drydock and Jetty Thickness Gauging on the Tees
description: Thickness gauging at Teesport and on the Tees: drydock UTM at the former Smith's Dock, tanker jetties, container feeders, ro-ro and bulk carriers at berth.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement at Teesport and the River Tees
intro: Teesport, on the south bank of the Tees estuary below Middlesbrough, is one of England's largest ports by tonnage and the working heart of an industrial river. Container feeders, ro-ro freight ships, bulk carriers and crude, chemical and gas tankers use berths along both banks, and the former Smith's Dock site is again a four-dock ship-repair yard. That combination brings both drydock gauging and in-service work at jetties and quays. Our technicians fly from India to Teesside for every ship.

highlights.h: Four drydocks at the old Smith's Dock
highlights.p: UK Docks operates four drydocks on the former Smith's Dock site at Teesport Commerce Park, taking offshore support vessels, dredgers, survey ships, tankers and naval vessels. A docking there gives the full window for tank-by-tank gauging worked alongside the yard and the class surveyor.

highlights.h: Tankers at the estuary's process jetties
highlights.p: Oil, chemical and gas jetties line the lower Tees. Ships at them stay briefly and work under strict terminal permits, so scopes centre on weather deck, cargo and ballast piping, and spaces the ship has already made gas-free and certified for entry.

highlights.h: Feeders and ro-ro on fixed rotations
highlights.p: Container feeders and ro-ro freight ships call at Teesport on regular schedules to Continental hubs. Their stays are short but predictable, so a gauging scope can be divided across consecutive calls without changing the timetable or holding the ship.

port.h: Teesport and the industrial Tees estuary
p: The Tees reaches the North Sea between Redcar and Hartlepool, with the South Gare breakwater guarding the entrance and a dredged channel leading upriver past chemical plants, oil terminals and steel quays towards Middlesbrough. PD Ports is the statutory harbour authority for the Tees and for Hartlepool, and runs Teesport itself on the south bank. Berths are spread over many miles of river on both banks, from the oil and chemical jetties near the mouth to the container terminal, bulk berths and general cargo quays further in. Pilotage is compulsory for most merchant ships, and the estuary's traffic is controlled by the harbour authority's vessel traffic service. An inspection team working several ships on the Tees in one visit therefore travels between berths by road rather than walking a single quay.

The traffic mirrors the industries along the river. Container feeders connect Teesport with the big Continental hubs, ro-ro freight ships run short-sea services to the near Continent, and steel, bulk and general cargo pass over the quays. Crude oil from the Norwegian Ekofisk area arrives by pipeline at the Seal Sands terminal and is shipped out by tanker, and the chemical and gas jetties at Seal Sands and North Tees serve the estuary's process plants. Bulk carriers use the deep-water bulk terminal at Redcar, built for the steelworks that closed in 2015, while the former steelworks land is being redeveloped for offshore wind manufacturing and port use. Offshore support vessels and dredgers come into the river for repair, and naval and government survey ships have docked at the yard.

There is no ice to plan around on the Tees, and the river is open throughout the year, but winter North Sea gales can close the entrance to small ships and delay arrivals. Deeper-draught tankers and bulk carriers time their passage up the channel to the tide, which can stretch a stay by hours. Ships waiting for a berth anchor in Tees Bay off the entrance. Next door, Hartlepool's docks handle general cargo and offshore work, and Able UK's Seaton Port, on the estuary near Hartlepool, has a large dry dock used for offshore decommissioning and ship recycling. Few estuaries in Britain give an inspection team such a range of ships, jetties and docks within a single short drive.

facilities.h: Drydocks, jetties and quays for gauging on the Tees
p: At UK Docks' yard on the former Smith's Dock site, a docking is the classic window for renewal or intermediate survey gauging. The yard's planners, the owner's superintendent and the class surveyor settle the TM plan before the ship arrives, the team works through tanks as they are cleaned, gas-freed and lit, and bottom and side shell are reached from the dock floor once the ship has settled on the blocks. Because the yard handles a lot of offshore support vessels, dredgers and survey ships, many dockings here involve thick-walled pipework and heavy deck equipment as well as plating, which we include in the plan rather than leaving for later.

On the jetties, the terminal sets the rules. A tanker at a Seal Sands or North Tees berth is worked under that terminal's permit system, which generally limits us to deck plating, cargo and ballast line wall thickness and any tanks the ship has certified gas-free. At the container, ro-ro and bulk berths the constraint is time rather than permits, so the scope is divided by space and spread across calls where the ship runs a regular service. Ships at the Tees Bay anchorage can be reached by launch through the agent when the weather allows, for a short deck and tank programme.
list: UK Docks, former Smith's Dock site at Teesport Commerce Park: four drydocks for renewal and docking survey gauging.
Seal Sands and North Tees jetties: deck, piping and gas-free tank gauging on oil, chemical and gas tankers within terminal permits.
Teesport container and ro-ro berths: scopes split across repeat calls on feeders and freight ships.
Bulk and steel berths, including the Redcar bulk terminal: hold, hopper and hatch-cover gauging during discharge.
Tees Bay anchorage: launch-borne gauging on ships waiting for a berth, when the weather allows.

context.h: Port state control, vetting and recycling rules on Teesside
p: Port state control on the Tees is carried out by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency within the Paris MoU, and the estuary's mix of older tankers and bulk carriers means expanded inspections are common. Tanker owners also face commercial vetting: oil majors inspect through OCIMF's SIRE 2.0 programme and chemical shippers through the Chemical Distribution Institute, and inspectors under both schemes look for evidence that hull and tank condition is known and managed. For a ship over fifteen years old trading to these jetties, a recent thickness record, or a Condition Assessment Programme rating where charterers ask for it, is part of staying employable.

The Tees is also one of the places in Britain where ships end their lives. Under the UK's ship recycling regulations, UK-flagged ships must carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and ships that also trade to EU ports need one under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation; the Hong Kong Convention, in force internationally since June 2025, adds the same requirement for ships of its parties. Owners weighing whether an older ship is worth another renewal survey or should go for recycling usually want a condition gauging first, because the steel renewal estimate is often what decides it.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Teesport
jobs.p: Work on the Tees divides between the yard and the berths. In dock, we follow the agreed TM plan beside the surveyor and pass findings to the yard as they are found, so renewal can be decided while the ship is still dry. At the berths, the job is shaped either by a terminal's permits or by a liner schedule. Requests come from superintendents of offshore and dredging fleets docking here, from tanker and bulk carrier managers whose ships call regularly, and from owners making repair or recycle decisions on older tonnage.
list: Renewal survey gauging on an offshore support vessel or dredger in dock at UK Docks' Tees yard, tank by tank to the agreed plan.
Chemical tanker at a Seal Sands berth: deck plating, cargo and ballast line wall thickness, and cofferdams gauged within the terminal's permit.
Container feeder on a weekly rotation: hatch cover and coaming plating, lashing bridge foundations and ballast tanks split across consecutive calls.
Bulk carrier at the Redcar terminal: hold frames, hopper plating and topside tanks gauged as each hold is emptied.
Condition gauging on an older tanker whose owner is deciding between another renewal survey and recycling.
Pre-docking steel estimate at a Tees berth for a ship booked into the yard on a later visit.

logistics: Teesside International Airport, near Darlington, is the closest airport but has a limited route network; Newcastle International has more connections and is within reach by road or rail. Middlesbrough has rail links to the national network. Teams travel from India on UK visit visas, so for a docking we fix travel once the yard confirms the slot. Access to PD Ports' berths and to the oil and chemical terminals is ISPS-controlled and arranged through the ship's agent, with terminal inductions where required; yard passes come through UK Docks.
vessels: Offshore support vessels and dredgers in refit

faqs.q: Do you gauge ships docked at the UK Docks yard on the Tees?
faqs.a: Yes, working for the owner or manager of the docked ship. We settle the TM plan with the attending class surveyor before the ship reaches the Tees, and the superintendent arranges tank cleaning, ventilation, staging and lighting with the yard. During the docking, readings showing substantial or excessive corrosion are reported as they are found, so steel renewal can be added to the yard's work list while the ship is dry.

faqs.q: Can a ship be gauged at the Tees Bay anchorage?
faqs.a: Yes, by launch arranged through the ship's agent, when the sea state allows safe boarding. Tees Bay is open to the north-east, so anchorage work suits a short, well-prepared scope: weather deck, air pipes, hatch covers and tanks the crew has opened in advance. We set priorities with the superintendent so the most important readings are taken first if the ship is called to its berth early.

faqs.q: How do you gauge a container feeder that only stays a few hours?
faqs.a: By splitting the scope across calls. A feeder on a weekly rotation to Teesport can have one or two ballast tanks, a set of hatch covers and part of the deck done each visit, with the crew preparing the next spaces before the following call. The readings are combined into one report on the class formats, so the owner ends up with a complete survey without the ship missing a sailing.

faqs.q: Can you help an owner decide whether an older ship is worth repairing?
faqs.a: We provide the condition data that decision rests on. A condition gauging before the next renewal survey shows where plating and stiffeners are close to their allowable diminution, and from that the owner and yard can estimate the steel renewal involved. That estimate, set against the ship's earnings prospects, is usually what tips the choice between another survey cycle and recycling.
